## It stops being so sure of itself

Eleven commits, and the one that matters most is the one that makes the
device *less* confident.

Every previous release treated confidence as a property of the detection
type. All twenty-nine FLOCK prefixes therefore carried the same grade —
including the sixteen that are generic Espressif blocks, present because
Flock build on ESP32. So every dev board, smart plug and hobby project in
range read as an ALPR camera with exactly the certainty of a real one. Two
SquachWatches in the same room would flag each other.

So every OUI in the firmware was checked against the IEEE MA-L registry
itself, rather than against other detectors — which is how the last bad
entry got in.

### What the audit found

Of the twenty-nine prefixes filed under FLOCK, **exactly one is registered
to Flock Safety**: `B4:1E:52`. Nine are Liteon. Sixteen are Espressif. One
is Shenzhen Intellirocks, one is a company called SPECTRA - TEK that had
been labelled "Flock-Sierra" and is neither Sierra nor Flock, one is not in
the registry at all, and one is a locally-administered address, which by
construction identifies nobody.

Elsewhere: a block labelled Hikvision belongs to Amazon. A block labelled
Reolink belongs to Hikvision. One Verkada block had been entered twice,
dead on arrival because the lookup returns on the first hit. And four
vendor labels were one character too long for the field they land in, so
the log had quietly been showing "Flock-ESP-S" for a while.

The worst of them shipped in v1.5.19 and earlier: `00:0E:58`, documented as
Vigilant, is registered to **Sonos, Inc.** of Goleta, California, assigned
February 2004. Every Sonos speaker in range was being logged as a licence
plate reader. It was removed rather than corrected, because there was
nothing to correct it to; seven blocks read straight out of the registry
took its place — four Motorola Solutions, two Genetec, and Verkada filed
under CAMERA rather than overstated as a plate reader.

### The rows all stay

None of the Espressif prefixes were deleted. An Espressif prefix **is**
evidence — Flock really do build on ESP32 — it is just evidence shared with
everything else on earth. Saying so is the difference between a detector
and a rumour.

What changed is that the grade now belongs to the matched signature rather
than to the type:

| Grade | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **High** | Registered to the company that makes the product |
| **Medium** | Registered to a parent whose range is far wider — Amazon owns Ring, and also Echo, Fire TV and Kindle |
| **Low** | A module or ODM vendor whose parts are in everything, or a block not in the registry |

Seventy-three rows: 31 High, 4 Medium, 38 Low.

**The payoff is larger than the bug.** ALERT FILTER has always been a
minimum-confidence filter with nothing to filter on, because confidence was
constant per type. It works now. Set it to High and a passing ESP32 stays
in the log without taking over the screen.

## Where the drone is, and where the pilot is standing

DRONE has always been a presence flag: `0xFFFA` is in the advert, so
something compliant is overhead. That advert also carries a 25-byte ASTM
F3411 message saying which aircraft it is, where it is — and, in the System
message, **where its operator is standing**.

Everything else this device finds tells you that a thing is nearby. This
tells you where the person holding it is.

The three message types arrive as separate adverts, so the decoder
accumulates per MAC and resets when a different aircraft starts talking:
half of one drone merged onto half of another would read as a plausible
aircraft that does not exist. The serial number names the log row, and MORE
INFO shows real coordinates instead of a general paragraph about what
Remote ID is.

Scope, stated honestly: **Bluetooth Legacy only.** Bluetooth 5 Long Range
is permanently out of reach on this board — the ESP32-WROOM is BLE 4.2 and
Espressif document no hardware support for Coded PHY or extended
advertising.

## iBeacons, which were being actively thrown away

Apple's format is `4C 00 02 15`, a 16-byte proximity UUID, a major, a minor
and a measured-power byte. Twenty-five bytes, every one fixed by the spec,
so this is an exact match rather than a judgement call like the AirTag
heuristic beside it.

They were not merely unsupported before. Apple's company ID matched the
AirTag rule, the payload check correctly said "not a tag", and the advert
was dropped — so the most numerous tracking transmitter most people walk
past all day was the one thing the detector was deliberately discarding.

The log row shows six hex of the proximity UUID, then major.minor. The UUID
is the *deployment*, shared by every beacon a chain owns, so the same first
half in two different places is the same operator, which is the part worth
seeing.

**Off by default, and it is the only type that is.** Not a judgement about
importance — about volume. One shop can put more beacons in range than this
device would otherwise see in a week. One tap away in DETECTION FILTER.

Found while wiring it up: the type mask was a `uint16_t` and this took the
count to seventeen. Bit 16 does not exist in a `uint16_t`, so the last type
would have shifted into undefined behaviour and silently vanished.

## Delete the last ignored device and have it stay deleted

Put one device on the IGNORE list, delete it, reboot, and it was back. It
reproduced at exactly one device and nowhere else.

`Preferences::putBytes` returns early on a zero-length value, before the
write and before the commit — so saving an empty list did nothing at all,
and the key kept the blob it already had, still holding the device just
deleted. In-memory state was correct the whole time: the count was zero and
the row was gone from the screen. The lie was only on flash, which is why
it took a reboot to see. Removing one of three devices writes 14 bytes and
one of two writes 7; only the removal that empties the list trips the
guard.

The emulator could not have caught it — its Preferences shim stored a
zero-length blob happily, so emptying the list worked there while failing
on hardware. The shim now reproduces the early return, because a shim more
forgiving than the hardware hides exactly the bugs the emulator exists to
find.

## A clock, at last

Every timestamp was counting from boot. A log row reading `71581:47` is
71581 minutes of uptime — an ordering, and nothing else — and the diary,
which is meant to be a record of days, could not name one.

There is no network sync, and that is deliberate: this device puts its
radio into promiscuous mode and never associates with an access point. SNTP
would mean asking for WiFi credentials, building somewhere to type them,
and going deaf for several seconds. That is a feature in its own right.

So the clock is **set** rather than synced, over the serial port the
project already documents at 2,000,000 baud:

```
TIME 1757331600
```

One line, no handshake — meant to be typed into a monitor or piped from
`date +%s`. It is backed by `settimeofday`, which is what makes it survive
a reboot: the ESP32 keeps system time across a software reset, so a
watchdog or a panic does not take the time with it. Power loss does, and
then it says so — unset, everything falls back to uptime exactly as before
rather than inventing a date.

Diagnostics gains UPTIME and CLOCK, next to RESET, because together those
three answer "did this thing restart on me", which is one question.

## Squachy

**A SIZE row** — SMALL, MEDIUM, LARGE at 70, 85 and 100 percent, LARGE by
default, so a board that has never been told otherwise draws him exactly as
before. CLEAR screen only: everywhere else he is a cameo in a box somebody
sized on purpose, and shrinking him there would just leave a hole. The
whole trick is anchoring from the *bottom*, so his soles stay planted on
the counters and the difference comes off the top.

**A bigger splash.** He was using 94 of the roughly 150 usable rows, with
the rest sitting as air above his head. Now 114 — about a fifth taller.
Both his scale and his standing line had to move together, because his
speech bubble sits a fixed distance above his head anchor and scaling him
alone drives it up into the subtitle.

## Also

**A BLACK background, in boring mode only.** Boring mode already strips
Squachy, the pet and the idle flourishes, but never touched the backdrop —
so "boring" still meant a screen full of falling glyphs. It is only in the
ring while boring mode is on, because the person who turned the mascot off
is the only one who would go looking for it. Turning boring mode off moves
you back to DIGITAL, and so does boot, since a saved BLACK would otherwise
strand the device on a flat screen with no way to cycle out.

**THE GIBSON on two screens that skipped it.** Selecting it and then
opening DETECTION FILTER or POWER SAVER gave you digital rain instead. Not
an oversight in those switches so much as a consequence: no file has an
explicit DIGITAL case — it *is* the default arm — so any value nobody
handled silently becomes rain rather than failing. Those two screens took
no detection engine, and the Gibson genuinely needs one: its skyline reads
the log and the trace across the bottom is live per-channel activity.

**Camera glasses beyond Ray-Ban.** The old signature caught Ray-Ban Meta
and nothing else. Meta Platforms, Meta Platforms Technologies, Luxottica
and Snap company IDs are in now, and the counter reads GLASS rather than
META, since Snap Spectacles are not Meta. META drops from High to Medium as
a result — Meta put those same IDs on Quest headsets, so the alert might be
a VR headset in a bag, and MORE INFO now says so.

**MORE INFO is honest again**, and can go stale less easily. Two panels
were describing the detection as it used to be. The text is indexed by type
and out-of-range clamps to zero, so a type with no entry showed UNKNOWN's
paragraph — wrong, plausible, and invisible until somebody tapped it. That
is a build error now.

**Host tests, and CI runs them.** Five suites in `test/`, no framework, run
with `make -C test`. They cover the decoders, which are the code most worth
testing and the least likely to tell you when they are wrong: a bad offset
in a coordinate field produces a plausible position somewhere else in the
world, not a crash. One suite is a round trip against SquachEmit, a
separate repository broadcasting the signatures this one matches — the two
have to agree byte for byte about a format neither owns, and nothing
checked that. It deliberately *copies* SquachEmit's packet building rather
than calling it, so editing either side without the other turns the test
red.

They earned their place immediately: the label test caught the four
truncated vendor names, and the new ignore-list suite was written by
reverting the fix to watch it fail.

**The emulator knows about all of this.** Its profile table is a linear
search, so a type with no entry simply never renders — IBEACON could not
draw its log row, its alert, its colour or its info panel at all, and its
ALPR profile was still the Sonos block. It now runs the *same* Remote ID
decoder the firmware does, and `--info N` renders the MORE INFO panel for
any type, which was previously only ever visible on hardware. That is
exactly how two of those paragraphs went stale without anyone noticing.

### The actually-useful part

- **Added**: Remote ID decoding — aircraft position, altitude, serial, and the operator's location
- **Added**: iBeacon detection, off by default; enable it in DETECTION FILTER
- **Added**: camera-glasses signatures for Meta, Luxottica and Snap
- **Added**: a SIZE setting for Squachy — SMALL, MEDIUM or LARGE, on the CLEAR screen
- **Added**: a BLACK background, available while boring mode is on
- **Added**: UPTIME and CLOCK on diagnostics, and a `TIME <epoch>` serial command to set the clock
- **Added**: five host test suites, run in CI
- **Changed**: per-signature confidence, so ALERT FILTER on High actually filters
- **Changed**: the counter reads GLASS rather than META
- **Changed**: Squachy fills the boot splash — about a fifth taller
- **Fixed**: deleting the only device on the IGNORE list brought it back on the next reboot
- **Fixed**: `00:0E:58` was logging every Sonos speaker as a licence plate reader
- **Fixed**: blocks mislabelled Hikvision and Reolink, a duplicated Verkada row, and four vendor names truncated in the log
- **Fixed**: THE GIBSON rendered as digital rain on the DETECTION FILTER and POWER SAVER screens
- **Fixed**: two MORE INFO panels described detections as they used to work
- **Fixed**: the detection type mask could not hold the seventeenth type
